newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - World sugar production estimate.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - World sugar production estimate.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

In spite of falling production in Eastern Europe and the problems encountered by the Indian sugar industry world sugar production in 1996/97 is forecast to rise by 3.6 million tonnes this season.

Even if demand should grow at the same fast pace as last year and taking into account unrecorded consumption this estimate points to another addition to world sugar stocks and lower world market prices. However, one has to be careful not to repeat the mistakes of last season.

Production increases are expected in the main sugar exporting nations of Brazil, Thailand, South Africa and Australia which should greatly improve supplies of high quality raws. Even though part of the increase will be mopped up by higher US import demand there should still be more than enough raw sugar around especially if the Cuban crop should maintain its upward path.

The situation in the whites sector at first looks more critical with the EU and Indian crops expected to come down and possibly larger demand from the Russian Federation given the unsatisfactory indigenous crop and the fall in Ukrainian production.

However, one has to go deeper into detail. The fall in Indian production will have no consequences whatsoever on the country's trading position due to the excessively high stocks which already exist and the industry is already lobbying the government to release 2 million tonnes for export after the one million tonnes allowed last season.

This means that supplies of low quality whites may rise in spite of lower production. The fall in EU production is not pronounced enough to have any material impact on exports and the total shipped could be even higher than last season, depending on the carry-over of C sugar to 1997/98.

Also hopes for higher Russian demand could prove to be an illusion given the country's efforts to restrain imports to help the domestic industry and the lack of foreign exchange. Moreover, white sugar demand could fall given higher production in Turkey, lower requirements from the Near and Middle East and greater competition from countries such as Brazil.
This reveals that the situation is rather complex and that the slowdown in production growth need not necessarily mean stable world market prices.

One of the features of the world sugar industry in recent years has been the dwindling share produced from beet. In 1986/87 nearly 37 per cent of the world's total was derived from beet; in 1996/97 we expect the share to have fallen to no more than 29 per cent.

We believe this trend will continue as beet sugar is mostly produced in the industrialised countries. The trend could be reversed if there were a recovery in output in Eastern Europe, particularly in Russia, but this hardly appears to be on the cards at the moment.

Beet sugar production in the EU is likely to amount to some 16.9 million tonnes, raw value, or about 150,000 tonnes down on the year. This drop will be more than made up by an increase of 690,000 tonnes in West European countries outside the EU, mainly in Turkey and Yugoslavia.

Many things are still going wrong in Russia. As a consequence of a smaller area, adverse weather and a lack of the necessary inputs we put Russian output at 1.820 million tonnes compared with 2.239 million tonnes in 1995/96. The Ukraine has suffered from similar difficulties; consequently its crop will also be down.

Some countries in Eastern Europe are optimistic, however, with the Czech Republic looking for a 17 per cent increase and Poland expecting to produce about two million tonnes after 1.7 million tonnes last season.
Beet sugar production outside Europe is also expected to fall with output in the two largest non-European producers, the USA and China, likely to be down.

The situation in the cane sector is quite different. In Asia Thailand goes from record to record with another expected in 1996/97 while even though output in India is likely to drop by around one million tonnes it will still exceed domestic needs.
Production is expected to rise by about 0.5 million tonnes in Pakistan while the Indonesian government is still aiming to increase output so as to reduce import needs.

In the Americas Cuban output is expected to continue its recovery but a slight fall to 4.7 million tonnes is looked for in Mexico. There will also be a fall in the USA with several areas unable to match last season's output. A new record of 1.5 million tonnes is likely to be reached in Guatemala. Rapid growth continues in Brazil which is also expected to register a new record of no less than 15.0 million tonnes.

South Africa has recovered from its four year drought and is expecting a 46 per cent increase in output to 2.6 million tonnes. Australia is expected to notch up another record with 5.6 million tonnes.
